## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Kāḷakaṇṇijātaka* (Ja 83) belongs to the Ekanipāta of the Pali *Jātaka* collection [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. In the framing story set at the Jetavana monastery, the Buddha addresses the situation of a childhood friend of the householder Anāthapiṇḍika [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. The friend, named Kāḷakaṇṇi (meaning "Curse" or "Unlucky"), had fallen into destitution; Anāthapiṇḍika kindly took him in and entrusted him with the management of his household property, despite the derision and discomfort visitors expressed over his inauspicious name [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877].
To illustrate the value of true loyalty over superstitious prejudice about names, the narrative introduces the canonical verse incipit *Mitto have sattapadena hoti* ("A friend is he...") [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. In the concluding identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the Buddha reveals that in that former existence in Bārāṇasī, the faithful friend Kāḷakaṇṇi was Ānanda, while the merchant of Bārāṇasī (*Bārāṇasīseṭṭhi*) was the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1877]. The text is also indexed among the Jātaka verse collections cataloged by Anandajoti [Anandajoti 2010].
Neither SuttaCentral nor the automated text-reuse analyses of DharmaNexus identify any Pali-internal reuse or cross-language parallels in Sanskrit, Chinese, or Tibetan corpora [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four modern translations across four languages [SuttaCentral].
